children: At the 9th BW Sustainable World Conclave, industry leaders said AI can accelerate sustainability efforts, but reliable data, human verification and clear accountability remain critical

Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a tool for businesses seeking to improve sustainability. Still, industry leaders at the 9th BW Sustainable World Conclave stressed that technology cannot replace credible data, human judgement and organisational accountability. The discussion, titled “AI for Sustainability: Can We Trust the Data Enough to Act on It?”, brought together Mitika Bajpai, DGM Sustainability, Reliance Industries; Khusboo Oswal, Global Head of Carbon Management, TÜV SÜD AG; Abhejit Agarwal, Head - Sustainability & CSR, Axis Bank; Rajesh Vasudevan, Chief Corporate EHS and Sustainability, Cipla; and Swapnil Joshi, Director & Industry Principal - Sustainability & Climate Tech, Smart Infrastructure; Head APAC & India, Infosys. Urvi Shrivastav, Assistant Editor, BW Businessworld, chaired the session.

Opening the discussion, Shrivastav questioned whether businesses can trust AI-generated outputs when the underlying data is inaccurate or incomplete. She asked how companies can be sure that the output is accurate if the correct data is not being fed into the system. Mitika Bajpai, DGM Sustainability, Reliance Industries, said the ultimate objective is to derive value from data and create new opportunities and use cases. She cited supply-chain applications and sustainability reporting, where AI can pre-fill information while human teams verify the data.
Bajpai also discussed an AI chatbot trained on internal safety information that helps manufacturing-site workers access safety protocols and checklists.

Khusboo Oswal, Global Head of Carbon Management, TÜV SÜD AG, said the certification and verification sector is increasingly embedding AI into its processes. She described TÜV SÜD as a “gatekeeper for regulation and compliance” and an “enabler of trust and integrity”, while noting that AI can process repetitive evidence reviews and support digital measurement, reporting and verification.

For Abhejit Agarwal, Head - Sustainability & CSR, Axis Bank, AI should serve a defined business purpose rather than become an end in itself. Discussing Axis Bank's enterprise-level AI model, he said it is being applied across customer-facing and backend functions, including data validation, customer onboarding, risk and operations.“AI is not an end in itself,” Agarwal said, adding that it should “serve a purpose” and improve existing processes while the organisation continues to make the final decisions.

The panel placed particular emphasis on human oversight in regulated sectors. Rajesh Vasudevan, Chief Corporate EHS and Sustainability, Cipla, said the pharmaceutical industry operates through a maker-checker process, with AI potentially performing the maker role but the checker continuing to be human because of the possibility of hallucinations. “Ultimately, the governance or the accountability still lies with the organisation,” Vasudevan said.

He also shared an example in which he tested dust-explosion data across different AI models and received different values, underlining the risks of accepting AI-generated technical information without independent verification. Swapnil Joshi, Director & Industry Principal - Sustainability & Climate Tech, Smart Infrastructure; Head APAC & India, Infosys, challenged the idea that AI itself solves sustainability problems.

“It does not. I think AI enables solving sustainability problems,” Joshi said, stressing that data remains fundamental to the quality of AI outputs. He warned that incomplete, fragmented or disproportionate data can result in systems producing confident but incorrect answers. On the question of accountability, Joshi said responsibility exists both with those developing AI and those using it, including ensuring data integrity.

“The output is as good as the input,” he said, warning that poor-quality data can result in what he described as a “perfectly greenwashed output”. Joshi also highlighted the wider social and environmental implications of AI, including its energy footprint, employment and skills impact, and the need to ensure that the benefits of AI are distributed equitably.

The panel also examined agentic AI and the growing ability of systems to perform tasks with limited human intervention. Speakers stressed that as AI becomes more autonomous, organisations will need clear governance frameworks defining responsibility among developers, users and decision-makers. The discussion ultimately highlighted a common principle: AI can accelerate sustainability efforts, but reliable data, human oversight and organisational accountability remain essential to ensuring that technology delivers credible outcomes.
